subject: bifactor CFA warning messages negative variances

messages.author: 26aafa36184ab4a9
messages.subject: bifactor CFA warning messages negative variances
parts:
Hi,

I would like to test a bifactor CFA model using lavaan, but I cannot eliminate negative variances and could not find the way to clear code to have a better model without warning messages.
(I did not have any issue in MPlus, where I received the following results: CFI = .980, TLI = .960, RMSEA = .080, df = 18, chi-square test: 46.016. I used MLR estimation there too.)
I used the following code in R:

# STUDY 1 - bifactor CFA
# model 
model_G <- '
fac1      =~  NA*item1 + item2 + item5
fac2      =~  NA*item3 + item4 + item7
fac3      =~  NA*item6 + item8 + item9
G         =~  NA*item1 + item2 + item5 + item3 + item4 + item7 + item6 + item8 + item9
G         ~~ 0*fac1
G         ~~ 0*fac2
G         ~~ 0*fac3
fac1      ~~ 0*fac2
fac1      ~~ 0*fac3
fac2      ~~ 0*fac3
G         ~~ 1*G
fac1      ~~ 1*fac1
fac2      ~~ 1*fac2
fac3      ~~ 1*fac3
'

# fit, summary, values
fit_G <- cfa(model_G, data = study1, estimator = 'MLR', optim.force.converged = TRUE)
summary(fit_G, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

As you can see, I used "optim.force.converged = TRUE" because without it I received the following warning message:
Warning message:
In .local(object, ...) :
  lavaan WARNING: fit measures not available if model did not converge


Adding "optim.force.converged = TRUE" helped me to run the code, while I received even more warning messages:
Warning messages:
1: In lav_model_estimate(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavpartable = lavpartable,  :
  lavaan WARNING: the optimizer warns that a solution has NOT been found!
2: In lav_model_hessian(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING: Hessian is not fully symmetric. Max diff = 6.38485562376445e-06
3: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel2, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)
    does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue
    (= -7.108829e-05) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that
    the model is not identified.
4: In lav_object_post_check(object) :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated ov variances are negative
> 

Do you have any suggestions how to modify my code to solve this issue in R?
I attached the relevant part of the data file and my code too. I hope it helps to reproduce the issue.

Thanks a lot for your suggestions in advance.
Janos

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: bifactor CFA warning messages negative variances
parts:
I used "optim.force.converged = TRUE" because without it I received the following warning message:
Warning message:
In .local(object, ...) :
  lavaan WARNING: fit measures not available if model did not converge

That is not a good reason to use that argument.  It does not make your model converge, it simply tells lavaan to lie to you.  Read the description on the ?lavOptions help page:

logical. If TRUE, pretend the model has converged, no matter what.

You should only use this option if you know how to obtain useful information from the nonconverged model to help you resolve the convergence problem.
Do you have any suggestions how to modify my code to solve this issue in R?

You can try leaving out the general factor to see if the model converges, or leaving out the method factors to see if that model converges.  You could also fix all general-factor loadings to 1, rather than estimate them.  Regardless, since some of your syntax is redundant with the std.lv=TRUE option, but I don't think that would be causing problems.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: 26aafa36184ab4a9
messages.subject: Re: bifactor CFA warning messages negative variances
parts:
Terrence, thanks a lot for your quick reply and suggestions.
I felt (and now see it why) that using forced converge is not a good practice, I deleted it from the code.

I also cleared the redundancies: I defined std.lv=TRUE instead of fixing covariances to zero on by one. Lavaan tutorial states that "If the argument std.lv=TRUE is used, the factor loadings of the first indicator of each latent variable will no longer be fixed to 1."
If I understand it right, defining each factor loading as unknown (pre-multiplying with NA) is also a redundancy, so I deleted them too.
After these modifications, using this code:

# STUDY 1 - bifactor CFA
# model 
model_G <- '

fac1      =~  item1 + item2 + item5
fac2      =~  item3 + item4 + item7
fac3      =~  item6 + item8 + item9
G         =~  item1 + item2 + item5 + item3 + item4 + item7 + item6 + item8 + item9

G         ~~ 1*G
fac1      ~~ 1*fac1
fac2      ~~ 1*fac2
fac3      ~~ 1*fac3
'
# fit, summary, values
fit_G <- cfa(model_G, data = study1, estimator = 'MLR', std.lv=TRUE)
summary(fit_G, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

I still receive the following warning messages:
Warning messages:
1: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel2, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :

lavaan WARNING:
    The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)
    does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue
(= -2.757799e-04) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that
the model is not identified.
2: In lav_object_post_check(object) :
lavaan WARNING: some estimated ov variances are negative

Leaving out either the general factor or the method factors works, the models converge without warning messages. Fixing all general-factor loadings to 1 leads a not converged model again.

The fit indices of the above showed bifactor model are much better (CFI = .990, TLI = .970, RMSEA = .069, df = 12, chi-square test: 25.870) than the first-order, second-order, or the general factor only models.
And the following MPlus code works without any problem, and gives the following results: CFI = .980, TLI = .960, RMSEA = .080, df = 18, chi-square test: 46.016

 ANALYSIS:
      estimator = mlr;
  !only for sample 1
      iteration = 10000;
      h1iteration = 10000;
      convergence = .05;
      h1convergence = .05;

 MODEL:
      global BY item2* item1 item3 item4 item5 item6 item7 item8 item9;

      fac1 BY item1* item2 item5;
      fac2 BY item3* item4 item7;
      fac3 BY item6* item8 item9;

      global@1; fac1@1; fac2@1; fac3@1;

      global-fac3 WITH global-fac3@0;


Unfortunately, I still do not know what makes the difference between the MPlus and R results, maybe fixing the problems suggested in the warning messages would solve the issue.

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: bifactor CFA warning messages negative variances
parts:
You must make sure that the 'specific' factors are uncorrelated with the
'global' factor. In Mplus, you had the syntax line

global-fac3 WITH global-fac3@0;

which sets ALL covariances to zero. In lavaan, you can either write

global ~~ 0*fac1 + 0*fac2 + 0*fac3
fac1 ~~ 0*fac2 + 0*fac3
fac2 ~~ 0*fac3

or use the orthgonal = TRUE argument.

Yves.

2019. október 22., kedd 12:08:36 UTC+2 időpontban Yves Rosseel a következőt írta:
You must make sure that the 'specific' factors are uncorrelated with the
'global' factor. In Mplus, you had the syntax line

global-fac3 WITH global-fac3@0;

which sets ALL covariances to zero. In lavaan, you can either write

global ~~ 0*fac1 + 0*fac2 + 0*fac3
fac1 ~~ 0*fac2 + 0*fac3
fac2 ~~ 0*fac3

or use the orthgonal = TRUE argument.

Yves.

parts:
Hi János,

As Terrence indicated, bifactor models have an unfortunate tendency to display convergence issues (and sometimes converged models have obviously incorrect estimates). Depending on the reason you are fitting the bifactor model, there are a number of ways to overcome this problem:

(1) You can leave off a specific factor or even just a single item (and, if you like, allow the other specific factors to correlate). This is the approach of Eid et al. (2017). This approach is reasonable when one of the specific factors can reasonably be expected to be trivial because its content is so closely aligned with the general factor.

(2) If your purpose is checking if your data is unidimensional to be treated as such (per Rodriguez, Reise, & Haviland, 2016), then if you accept the three factor model as fitting acceptably, you can reparameterize it into a special case of bifactor model called a "testlet" model. You can either directly compute the coefficients from the three factor model, or you can fit a model in which factor loadings are constrained to be equal in the general and specific factors, the general factor variance is fixed to one, and the specific factor variances are freely estimated. 

Note that this approach is only reasonable for two or three factor models (testlet models are statistically equivalent to second order factor models, and two- and three- factor correlated traits models are always statistically equivalent to second order factor models).

(3) If you plan on using a total sum score eventually, then you can follow Terrence's suggestion above and fix all the loadings of the general factor to one.

(4) If you are willing to switch to a Bayesian framework you have some more choices

(5) You can resolve the convergence issue in a number of other creative ways, but you'd be hard pressed to argue that other techniques are reasonable.

It has been my personal, anecdotal experience (i.e., take this with a grain of salt) that misfit is often to blame for bifactor models having convergence issues. To diagnose if this is actually the case, I would fit a unidimensional model and look at the residual correlation matrix. The within specific factor residual correlation should be large and the across specific factor residual correlations should be small.

-David

Eid, M., Geiser, C., Koch, T., & Heene, M. (2017). Anomalous results in G-factor models: Explanations and alternatives. Psychological Methods, 22(3), 541.
Rodriguez, A., Reise, S. P., & Haviland, M. G. (2016). Evaluating bifactor models: calculating and interpreting statistical indices. Psychological Methods, 21(2), 137.
